prompt: What is evaporation?

choices.text: The formation of a gas from a liquid at temperatures below its boiling point
A liquid turning into a gas at its boiling point
choices.why: That is boiling. Evaporation happens below the boiling point, as particles at the surface with enough energy escape.

choices.text: A gas turning into a liquid
choices.why: That is condensation, the reverse of evaporation.

choices.text: A solid turning directly into a gas
choices.why: That is sublimation. Evaporation starts from a liquid.

explanation: Every liquid has some particles with enough energy to enter the gas phase, and those at the surface do so. The formation of a gas from a liquid below its boiling point is called evaporation.

prompt: Water evaporating from a glass at room temperature forms water vapor. Why does the section call it vapor rather than gas?

choices.text: The term gas is reserved for when the gas phase is the stable phase; below the boiling point, the material in the gas phase is called vapor.
Vapor is made of tiny liquid droplets, not separate molecules.
choices.why: Vapor is in the gas phase: separate molecules. The name only signals that the liquid is the stable phase at that temperature.

choices.text: Vapor is a different chemical substance from the liquid.
choices.why: Evaporation is a physical change, so water vapor is still H2O.

choices.text: Only water forms vapor; other liquids form gases.
choices.why: All liquids evaporate and form vapor below their boiling points.

explanation: At temperatures below the boiling point, the material in the gas phase is called vapor rather than gas; the term gas is reserved for when the gas phase is the stable phase.

prompt: Which liquids evaporate?

choices.text: All liquids
Only water
choices.why: Every liquid has some particles with enough energy to escape from its surface, so every liquid evaporates.

choices.text: Only liquids that are above their boiling points
choices.why: Evaporation happens below the boiling point. Above it, the liquid boils.

choices.text: Only liquids with weak intermolecular forces
choices.why: Weak forces make a liquid evaporate faster, but even liquids with strong forces have some particles energetic enough to escape.

explanation: All liquids have a certain portion of particles with enough energy to enter the gas phase, so all liquids evaporate.

prompt: A small amount of a liquid is left in a very large space, so the available volume is far more than the vapor could fill. What eventually happens?

choices.text: All of the liquid becomes vapor.
Evaporation and condensation reach equilibrium, and some liquid always remains.
choices.why: Equilibrium is reached only when the available volume is limited. With enough space, the vapor never builds up enough to return to the liquid as fast as it leaves.

choices.text: Nothing; a liquid only evaporates at its boiling point.
choices.why: Liquids evaporate below their boiling points too.

choices.text: The liquid freezes, because evaporation takes energy away.
choices.why: The section describes the liquid evaporating until none is left when the available volume is large enough.

explanation: If the available volume is large enough, eventually all the liquid will become vapor. Only when the volume is limited do some vapor particles reenter the liquid and set up an equilibrium.

prompt: What is the vapor pressure of a liquid?

choices.text: The partial pressure of the vapor when it is in equilibrium with the liquid
The pressure needed to turn the vapor back into a liquid
choices.why: Vapor pressure is the pressure the vapor itself exerts at equilibrium, when particles leave and return to the liquid at the same rate.

choices.text: The total pressure of all the air above the liquid
choices.why: It's only the partial pressure of the substance's own vapor, at equilibrium with the liquid.

choices.text: The pressure of the vapor at the instant the liquid starts to evaporate
choices.why: Vapor pressure is measured at equilibrium, after the amount of vapor stops changing.

explanation: When the number of particles entering the vapor phase equals the number leaving it, the system is at equilibrium. The partial pressure of the vapor at equilibrium is the vapor pressure of the liquid.

prompt: A liquid sits in a sealed jar, and the amount of vapor above it has stopped changing. What is happening at the molecular level?

choices.text: Molecules are still evaporating, and vapor molecules are condensing back into the liquid at the same rate.
Evaporation has stopped, because the air above the liquid is full.
choices.why: The liquid has not stopped evaporating. Condensation now occurs just as fast, so there is no net change.

choices.text: Condensation has stopped, and evaporation continues slowly.
choices.why: If only evaporation continued, the amount of vapor would keep growing. Both processes continue at equal rates.

choices.text: All molecular motion has stopped.
choices.why: The molecules keep moving; evaporation and condensation simply balance each other.

explanation: This is a dynamic equilibrium: a process still occurs, but the opposite process occurs at the same rate, so there is no net change. The liquid keeps evaporating while the vapor condenses just as fast.

prompt: A student watching a closed bottle of water says: "The water level isn't changing any more, so the water has stopped evaporating." What is wrong?

choices.text: The water is still evaporating; vapor condenses back at the same rate, so the level stays the same.
Nothing is wrong; evaporation stops once the bottle is closed.
choices.why: Closing the bottle doesn't stop evaporation. It lets vapor build up until condensation keeps pace with evaporation.

choices.text: The level is actually still dropping, too slowly to see.
choices.why: At equilibrium there really is no net change; evaporation and condensation are balanced.

choices.text: Water only evaporates in open containers, so it never evaporated at all.
choices.why: Water evaporates in closed containers too, until a dynamic equilibrium is reached.

explanation: Understand that the liquid has not stopped evaporating. Condensation is occurring as fast as evaporation, so there is no net change in the amount of vapor: a dynamic equilibrium.

prompt: How does the vapor pressure of a liquid change as its temperature increases?

choices.text: It increases.
It decreases.
choices.why: At a higher temperature more particles have enough energy to escape, so the vapor pressure rises.

choices.text: It stays the same, because vapor pressure depends only on the identity of the liquid.
choices.why: Vapor pressure depends on both the identity of the liquid and the temperature.

choices.text: It increases until the liquid freezes.
choices.why: Freezing happens at low temperature. Vapor pressure rises with temperature, up to the point where the liquid boils.

explanation: The vapor pressure of a substance depends on its temperature: as the temperature increases, so does the vapor pressure.

prompt: Using vapor pressure, how does the section redefine the boiling point of a liquid?

choices.text: The temperature at which its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure
The temperature at which its vapor pressure is zero
choices.why: Vapor pressure is lowest at low temperatures. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure has risen to match the surrounding pressure.

choices.text: The temperature at which it starts to evaporate
choices.why: Liquids evaporate at temperatures well below their boiling points.

choices.text: The temperature at which its vapor pressure is twice the surrounding pressure
choices.why: Boiling starts as soon as the vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure.

explanation: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapor pressure equals the surrounding environmental pressure. The normal boiling point is the temperature at which the vapor pressure is 760 torr, or exactly 1 atm.

prompt: At a liquid's normal boiling point, its vapor pressure equals a standard surrounding pressure. What is that pressure in torr?
explanation: The normal boiling point is the temperature at which the vapor pressure of the liquid is 760 torr, or exactly 1 atm.

prompt: High on a mountain, the atmospheric pressure is lower than at sea level. How does this affect the boiling point of water there?

choices.text: Water boils at a lower temperature, because its vapor pressure reaches the lower surrounding pressure sooner.
Water boils at a higher temperature, because there is less air to help it boil.
choices.why: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure. Lower surrounding pressure is reached at a lower temperature.

choices.text: Water still boils at exactly 100°C, because that is water's boiling point.
choices.why: 100°C is the normal boiling point, at exactly 1 atm. Boiling points vary with the surrounding pressure.

choices.text: Water can't boil at high altitude.
choices.why: It boils; it just does so at a lower temperature, once its vapor pressure matches the lower surrounding pressure.

explanation: Because a liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure, and atmospheric pressure varies significantly with altitude, water boils at a lower temperature where the pressure is lower. This affects cooking at high elevations.

prompt: The surrounding pressure on a pot of water is raised above 1 atm. What happens to the temperature at which the water boils?

choices.text: It rises above 100°C, because the vapor pressure must climb higher to equal the surrounding pressure.
It falls below 100°C, because the extra pressure pushes the molecules into the gas phase.
choices.why: Higher surrounding pressure makes it harder to boil: the water must get hotter for its vapor pressure to match.

choices.text: It stays at 100°C, because pressure doesn't affect boiling.
choices.why: Boiling points vary with surrounding pressure; 100°C is water's boiling point only at exactly 1 atm.

choices.text: The water can no longer boil at any temperature.
choices.why: It still boils, once its vapor pressure rises to equal the higher surrounding pressure.

explanation: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure. Vapor pressure increases with temperature, so a higher surrounding pressure means the water must reach a higher temperature before it boils.

prompt: Does ice have a vapor pressure?

choices.text: Yes, though it is typically much lower than that of a liquid; that's why ice sublimes over time.
No; only liquids have vapor pressures.
choices.why: Solids have vapor pressures too. Ice's is small, but large enough that ice sublimes over time.

choices.text: Yes, and it is higher than liquid water's at the same temperature.
choices.why: The vapor pressures of solids are typically much lower than those of liquids.

choices.text: Only above 0°C.
choices.why: Ice has a vapor pressure below 0°C: 4.2 torr at −1°C and 1.0 torr at −17°C.

explanation: Even ice has a vapor pressure, which is why it sublimes over time. The vapor pressures of solids are typically much lower than those of liquids: ice's is 4.2 torr at −1°C.

prompt: The vapor pressure of ice is 4.2 torr at −1°C and only 1.0 torr at a freezer temperature of −17°C. How many times greater is ice's vapor pressure at −1°C than at −17°C?
explanation: 4.2 torr ÷ 1.0 torr = 4.2. The colder the ice, the lower its vapor pressure, which is why a colder freezer slows sublimation.

prompt: At a freezer temperature of −17°C, the vapor pressure of ice is 1.0 torr. What is this pressure in atmospheres? (1 atm = 760 torr.)
explanation: 1.0 torr × (1 atm / 760 torr) = 0.0013 atm, a tiny pressure compared with the vapor pressure of liquid water at room temperature.

prompt: A deep freezer at −23°C keeps food from developing freezer burn longer than a regular freezer at −17°C. Why?

choices.text: Ice's vapor pressure is lower at −23°C (0.6 torr) than at −17°C (1.0 torr), so it sublimes more slowly.
Ice can't sublime below −20°C.
choices.why: Ice still has a vapor pressure at −23°C (0.6 torr), so it still sublimes, only more slowly.

choices.text: At −23°C the ice melts more slowly.
choices.why: Ice doesn't melt in either freezer. Freezer burn comes from sublimation, which slows as the vapor pressure falls.

choices.text: Colder ice has a higher vapor pressure, which holds the water in place.
choices.why: It's the opposite: colder ice has a lower vapor pressure, so less water escapes as vapor.

explanation: The vapor pressure of ice falls with temperature: 1.0 torr at −17°C but only 0.6 torr at −23°C. With a lower vapor pressure, the ice in the food sublimes more slowly.

prompt: What causes surface tension?

choices.text: Particles at the surface feel intermolecular forces from the sides and below but not from above, so the forces on them are unbalanced.
A thin layer of a different substance forms on top of the liquid.
choices.why: No separate layer is needed. Surface tension comes from the liquid's own particles at the surface having no neighbors above them.

choices.text: The particles at the surface are covalently bonded to each other.
choices.why: Surface particles are held by the same intermolecular forces as the rest. The difference is that nothing pulls on them from above.

choices.text: Gravity pulls the surface particles down harder than the others.
choices.why: Gravity acts on all the particles. Surface tension comes from the imbalance of intermolecular forces at the surface.

explanation: A particle in the bulk of a liquid feels intermolecular forces from all around, but a particle at the surface has no particles above it. This imbalance of forces is called surface tension.

prompt: Which of these is caused by surface tension?

choices.text: Small insects can walk on the surface of water.
Water expands when it freezes.
choices.why: Water expands on freezing because hydrogen bonding lines the molecules up with empty space between them, not because of surface tension.

choices.text: Water boils at a lower temperature on a mountain.
choices.why: That comes from the lower surrounding pressure, which water's vapor pressure reaches at a lower temperature.

choices.text: Ice cubes shrink in a freezer.
choices.why: That is sublimation of the ice, not surface tension.

explanation: Because of surface tension, it takes energy to break the surface of a liquid. A small insect isn't heavy enough to break through, so it stays on top of the water. Surface tension also makes liquids bead up and form spheres in free fall or zero gravity.

prompt: A steel paper clip, carefully laid flat on water, can rest on the surface instead of sinking. Why?

choices.text: It takes energy to break the surface of the liquid, and the light paper clip doesn't push down hard enough to break through.
Steel is less dense than water.
choices.why: Steel is much denser than water; a paper clip dropped in edge-first sinks. It rests on top only because of surface tension.

choices.text: The paper clip dissolves slightly and becomes part of the surface.
choices.why: Steel doesn't dissolve in water. The surface holds the paper clip up because breaking through it takes energy.

choices.text: The paper clip repels water by adhesion.
choices.why: Adhesion is attraction, not repulsion. The paper clip is held up by surface tension.

explanation: Because of surface tension, it takes energy to break the surface of a liquid. If an object is light enough, there's not enough force from gravity to break through, so it stays on top. Carefully done, this works with a thin razor blade or a paper clip.

prompt: What is the difference between adhesion and cohesion?

choices.text: Adhesion is a substance's tendency to interact with other substances; cohesion is its tendency to interact with itself.
Adhesion is the tendency of a substance to interact with itself; cohesion is its tendency to interact with other substances.
choices.why: That has them reversed. Adhesion is attraction to other substances (like water to glass); cohesion is attraction within the substance.

choices.text: Adhesion happens only in solids; cohesion happens only in liquids.
choices.why: Both describe intermolecular attractions; for liquids, the balance between them decides whether a liquid beads up or spreads out.

choices.text: They are two names for surface tension.
choices.why: Surface tension is the imbalance of forces at a liquid's surface. Adhesion and cohesion compare a liquid's attraction to other substances with its attraction to itself.

explanation: Adhesion is the tendency of a substance to interact with other substances because of intermolecular forces, while cohesion is the tendency of a substance to interact with itself.

prompt: When does a liquid spread out over a surface, or wet it, instead of beading up?

choices.text: When the adhesive forces between the liquid and the surface are stronger than the cohesive forces within the liquid
When the cohesive forces within the liquid are stronger than the adhesive forces
choices.why: Stronger cohesion makes the liquid keep to itself and bead up.

choices.text: When the liquid has no intermolecular forces at all
choices.why: Every liquid has intermolecular forces. Wetting depends on which is stronger: attraction to the surface or attraction within the liquid.

choices.text: Only when the liquid is water
choices.why: Any liquid can wet a surface if its adhesion to that surface beats its cohesion.

explanation: If adhesive forces between a liquid and another substance are stronger than the cohesive forces within the liquid, the liquid spreads out to maximize its contact with the other substance: it wets it. If cohesion is stronger, the liquid beads up.

prompt: When a thin glass tube is dipped into water, the water rises up the tube and forms an upwardly curved surface. What explains this?

choices.text: Strong adhesion between water and glass pulls the water up the tube: capillary rise.
Strong cohesion within the water pushes it up the tube.
choices.why: Strong cohesion compared with adhesion gives capillary depression, as with mercury. Water rises because its adhesion to glass is strong.

choices.text: Air pressure inside the tube is lower than outside.
choices.why: The tube is open to the same air. The water rises because of its adhesion to the glass.

choices.text: The water evaporates and condenses higher up the tube.
choices.why: The water climbs as a liquid, drawn up by adhesion to the glass.

explanation: If adhesive forces are strong, a liquid in a small-diameter tube moves up the tube, as if ignoring gravity. This is capillary rise, and the water forms an upwardly curved surface called a meniscus.

prompt: When a thin glass capillary is placed in a pool of mercury, the mercury surface inside the tube is pushed down and its meniscus curves downward. Why?

choices.text: Mercury's cohesive forces are stronger than its adhesion to glass: capillary depression.
Mercury's adhesion to glass is stronger than its cohesion.
choices.why: Strong adhesion would pull the mercury up the tube, as with water. Mercury is pushed down because its cohesion is stronger.

choices.text: Mercury is too dense to have any intermolecular forces.
choices.why: Mercury has very strong cohesive forces; that's exactly what causes the depression.

choices.text: Mercury has no surface tension.
choices.why: All liquids have surface tension. Mercury's strong cohesion is what pushes it down in the capillary.

explanation: Some liquids have stronger cohesive forces than adhesive forces. In a capillary, such a liquid is forced down from its surface and its meniscus curves downward: capillary depression. Mercury has very strong cohesive forces.

prompt: Why are bath towels made of cotton rather than polyester or rayon?

choices.text: Cotton fibers form tiny capillaries with good adhesion to water, so they wick water away; synthetic fabrics don't show similar capillary action.
Cotton makes water evaporate faster.
choices.why: Towels dry you by soaking up water through capillary action, not by speeding evaporation.

choices.text: Water has strong cohesion with cotton.
choices.why: Cohesion is a substance's attraction to itself. Water's attraction to cotton is adhesion.

choices.text: Cotton has high surface tension.
choices.why: Surface tension is a property of liquids. Towels work by capillary action in the gaps between their fibers.

explanation: Capillary action is responsible for the wicking effect of towels and sponges: the matted fibers form tiny capillaries with good adhesion to water. Cotton is good at this; polyester and other synthetic fabrics are not, which is why rayon bath towels are rare.

prompt: Which of these does the section give as an example of capillary action?

choices.text: Melted wax climbing a candle's wick
Water beading up on an apple
choices.why: Beading up is caused by surface tension and cohesion, not by a liquid moving through narrow tubes.

choices.text: Ice cubes shrinking in a freezer
choices.why: That is sublimation.

choices.text: Water boiling at a lower temperature on a mountain
choices.why: That comes from the lower surrounding pressure, not from capillary action.

explanation: Capillary action is behind the wicking of towels and sponges, liquid fuels and melted wax rising in their wicks, and, at least partly, the transport of water from the roots to the tops of trees.

prompt: Water beads up on a freshly waxed car instead of spreading out. Why does this help protect the car from rust?

choices.text: Wax has low adhesion with water, so water beads up instead of wetting the surface, minimizing its contact with the metal.
Wax reacts with water and destroys it.
choices.why: No reaction takes place. Wax's long hydrocarbon molecules simply don't interact well with water.

choices.text: Wax has strong adhesion with water, so the water is held away from the metal.
choices.why: Strong adhesion would make water spread out and wet the surface. Wax works because its adhesion with water is low.

choices.text: Wax lowers water's cohesion, so the water runs off.
choices.why: Wax doesn't change water's cohesion. Water beads up because its cohesion beats its weak adhesion to the wax.

explanation: Wax is made of long hydrocarbon molecules that don't interact well with water. A freshly waxed car has low adhesive forces with water, so water beads up because of its cohesion and surface tension, which minimizes the contact between water and metal.

prompt: Why does dirty or scratched car paint promote rust more than clean, waxed paint?

choices.text: It can attract water, and adhesive forces let the water wet the surface, maximizing its contact with the metal.
Scratches increase the surface tension of the water.
choices.why: Surface tension is a property of the liquid. The problem is that water adheres to dirty or scratched paint and spreads over it.

choices.text: Dirt makes water's cohesion stronger, so it stays on the car longer.
choices.why: Stronger cohesion would make water bead up and touch less of the surface. Dirty paint attracts water, so adhesion lets it spread.

choices.text: Scratched paint is colder, so water condenses on it.
choices.why: The issue is adhesion: water wets dirty or scratched paint and spreads over it.

explanation: Water is an important factor in the rusting of iron. Dirty or scratched paint can attract water, and adhesive forces let the water wet the surface, maximizing its contact with the metal and promoting rust.
